issues.legal_issue: A statutory power to evict persons from municipal premises on grounds including unauthorised occupation does not violate equality guarantees when it concerns property belonging to government or a semi-government body and provides a hearing opportunity.
material_facts: The Chief Officer was empowered to order a person in unauthorised occupation of municipal premises to vacate.
Before making an eviction order, the Chief Officer had to give notice of the grounds and a reasonable opportunity to explain and produce evidence.
The person served with the eviction notice challenged the statutory eviction power as unconstitutional.
An appeal against an eviction order could be made to the Government, which could condone delay for sufficient cause.
issues.conclusion: The statutory eviction power was not invalid under Article 14; the High Court’s contrary judgment was set aside and the Chief Officer’s order was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, property belonging to government or semi-government bodies may constitute a reasonable class. Once that classification is reasonable, the absence of a civil remedy does not by itself make the eviction provision discriminatory. The Court relied on Chhaganlal Maganlal, which overruled Northern India Caterers’ contrary approach, and on Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram, which upheld a provision in pari materia. The availability of an administrative appeal was also noted.

issues.definition: When a constitutional validity challenge concerns an eviction power over government or semi-government property that includes a hearing opportunity, the eviction scheme survives equality review.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory scheme authorising eviction from municipal premises does not violate the constitutional freedom guarantees raised under Article 19.
material_facts: The statutory scheme empowered a municipal Chief Officer to order eviction from municipal premises, including where a person was in unauthorised occupation.
The scheme required notice of the proposed grounds and an opportunity to explain and produce evidence before an eviction order.
The affected person challenged the scheme under Article 19.
issues.conclusion: The Article 19 challenge was rejected, consistently with the Court’s decision in Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram, in which the contention that the relevant municipal eviction provisions violated Article 19 had been considered and rejected.
